name: Learning::NSW Year 9::Pythagoras::Question patterns
description: 32 cards on recognising and solving Pythagoras questions: ladders, wires, diagonals, routes, coordinates, ramps and hidden right triangles. Includes method-selection counterexamples and one labelled 3D extension. Every answer has an explanatory diagram. Attempt the words before revealing the model.

cards.front: A ladder leans against a vertical wall on level ground. Which length represents the hypotenuse?
cards.back: The ladder’s length: the ladder is opposite the right angle between wall and ground.

cards.front: A 13 m ladder leans against a vertical wall. Its foot is 5 m from the wall on level ground. How high does it reach?
A 10 m ladder reaches 8 m up a vertical wall. How far is its foot from the wall on level ground?
A taut wire joins the top of a 12 m vertical pole to an anchor 5 m from its base on level ground. Find the wire’s length.
cards.back: 13 m: the wire is the hypotenuse, so √(12² + 5²) = 13.

cards.front: A taut 20 m wire runs from a 16 m vertical pole’s top to level ground. How far from the pole’s base is the anchor?
A rectangular field is 8 m wide and 15 m long. Find the straight distance between opposite corners.
cards.back: 17 m: opposite corners are joined by the diagonal, √(8² + 15²).

cards.front: A square courtyard has side 7 m. Find its diagonal to one decimal place.
A rectangular sign has diagonal 25 cm and height 7 cm. Find its width.
A rectangular screen is 30 cm wide and 40 cm high. What is its corner-to-corner screen size?
cards.back: 50 cm: the diagonal follows the 3–4–5 pattern scaled by 10.

cards.front: You walk 6 km north, then 8 km east. How far are you from your starting point in a straight line?
cards.back: 10 km: north and east are perpendicular, so √(6² + 8²) = 10.

cards.front: You walk 6 km north, then 8 km east. Why is the distance you actually walked 14 km, not 10 km?
cards.back: Travel distance adds the route’s two legs: 6 + 8 = 14 km. Ten kilometres is the direct shortcut.

cards.front: A boat travels 9 km west, then 12 km north. Find its straight-line distance from the start.
cards.back: 15 km: west and north are perpendicular, and 9–12–15 is a scaled 3–4–5 triangle.

cards.front: On a square coordinate grid, A is (1, 2) and B is (7, 10). Find the straight-line distance AB.
cards.back: 10 units: horizontal change 6, vertical change 8; √(6² + 8²) = 10.

cards.front: On a square coordinate grid, P is (−3, 1) and Q is (5, 7). Find PQ.
A straight ramp rises 0.9 m vertically over a horizontal run of 1.2 m. Find the ramp’s length.
cards.back: 1.5 m: the ramp is the hypotenuse, √(0.9² + 1.2²).

cards.front: A straight ramp is 5 m long and rises 3 m vertically. Find its horizontal run.
cards.back: 4 m: run = √(5² − 3²). The 5 m ramp is the hypotenuse.

cards.front: A ramp rises 3 m over a horizontal run of 4 m. In “find the length of the ramp”, which triangle side is requested?
cards.back: The sloping hypotenuse, not the vertical rise or horizontal run.

cards.front: An isosceles tent cross-section has equal sloping sides 10 m and base 12 m. Find its perpendicular height.
cards.back: 8 m: the height halves the base to 6 m, so h = √(10² − 6²).

cards.front: Find the perpendicular height of an equilateral triangle of side 10 cm, to one decimal place.
cards.back: 8.7 cm: half the base is 5 cm; h = √(10² − 5²) = √75 ≈ 8.6603.

cards.front: A rhombus has diagonals 6 cm and 8 cm. They bisect each other at right angles. Find one side of the rhombus.
cards.back: 5 cm: use half-diagonals 3 cm and 4 cm as the legs; √(3² + 4²) = 5.

cards.front: An isosceles triangle has equal sides 13 cm and base 10 cm. Find its area.
Extension: a rectangular box measures 12 cm by 9 cm by 8 cm. Find the internal diagonal joining opposite corners through the box.
cards.back: 17 cm: base diagonal = 15 cm; space diagonal = √(15² + 8²) = 17.

cards.front: A tree is 10 m from a bench on a straight path. Its perpendicular foot on the path is 6 m from the bench. Find the shortest tree-to-path distance.
cards.back: 8 m: the shortest distance is perpendicular to the path, so √(10² − 6²) = 8.

cards.front: A rectangular garden is 6 m by 8 m. How much fencing goes around its boundary? Decide whether Pythagoras is needed.
cards.back: 28 m: perimeter = 2(6 + 8). Pythagoras is unnecessary because no diagonal is requested.

cards.front: Two sides of a triangle are 8 cm and 10 cm, with 60° between them. Why can’t you use 8² + 10² to find the third side’s square?
cards.back: The included angle is 60°, not 90°. Those sides are not perpendicular legs.

cards.front: A right triangle has hypotenuse 10 cm and an acute angle of 35°. Which method directly finds the opposite side, and why?
cards.back: Trigonometry: sine uses an angle and the hypotenuse. Pythagoras needs two known side lengths.

cards.front: A parallelogram has adjacent sides 6 cm and 8 cm and an included angle of 60°. Why can’t you assume its diagonal is 10 cm?
cards.back: A parallelogram need not have right angles. The 6–8–10 shortcut requires perpendicular 6 cm and 8 cm sides.

cards.front: An isosceles triangle has two 12 cm sides. What extra fact would justify using 12² + 12² to find its third side’s square?
cards.back: The angle between the two 12 cm sides must be 90°.

cards.front: A rectangular board is 5 cm by 7 cm. Find its diagonal to the nearest tenth of a centimetre.
cards.back: 8.6 cm: d = √74 ≈ 8.6023, rounded only at the end.

cards.front: A 250 cm ladder leans against a vertical wall, with its foot 1.5 m away on level ground. Find its vertical reach in metres.
cards.back: 2 m: convert 250 cm to 2.5 m, then √(2.5² − 1.5²) = 2.

cards.front: A rectangular gate is 2.4 m wide and 1.8 m high. Find the length of a straight brace from one corner to the opposite corner.
cards.back: 3 m: the brace is the diagonal; use 3–4–5 scaled by 0.6.

cards.front: A builder measures a triangular layout: 9 m, 12 m and 15 m. Explain how this checks whether the 9 m and 12 m edges meet at 90°.
cards.back: 9² + 12² = 15². The converse of Pythagoras confirms a right angle between the shorter edges.
